title: J.P. Morgan Chase v. City of Corsicana
description: Whether economic-development grants authorized by section 52-a of the Texas Constitution are exempt from the traditional Gift Clause requirements, or if they remain subject to scrutiny regarding public purpose, controls, and non-gratuitous expenditure.
plaintiff_argument: JPMorgan Chase argued that section 52-a's "notwithstanding" clause exempts economic development grants from the pre-existing Gift Clause requirements.
defendant_argument: The City of Corsicana and Navarro County argued that section 52-a only establishes economic development as a public purpose within the traditional Gift Clause framework, meaning the grants are still subject to Gift Clause requirements, and that the closure of Gander Mountain extinguished the public purpose, making continued payments unconstitutional.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the lower courts' summary judgment, holding that economic-development grants under section 52-a are subject to Gift Clause requirements but that the closure of a specific business does not automatically extinguish the public purpose if broader economic development continues, and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: Muth v. Voe; Doe v. Abbott; Muth v. PFLAG
description: Whether the injunctions preventing the Texas Department of Family and Protective Services from classifying gender-transition therapy for children as child abuse should be dissolved.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs (families, PFLAG, and Dr. Mooney) argued that the injunctions should remain because DFPS's classification of gender-transition therapy for children as child abuse violates the law and infringes on rights.
defendant_argument: The defendants (DFPS, Commissioner Muth, and Governor Abbott) argued that the injunctions should be dissolved because DFPS's classification is lawful and constitutional, and the underlying claims are moot or lack standing.
decision_outcome: The court dissolved the injunctions that prevented the Texas Department of Family and Protective Services from classifying gender-transition therapy for children as child abuse.

title: PFLAG v. Office of the Attorney General
description: Whether the Attorney General's Civil Investigative Demand (CID) to PFLAG for documents related to an investigation into deceptive billing practices concerning transgender treatments for minors (SB 14) is valid and enforceable, with PFLAG arguing it is overly broad and infringes on privacy, and the Attorney General arguing it is a reasonable and necessary investigatory tool.
plaintiff_argument: PFLAG argued that the CID was overly broad, sought privileged information, and was not relevant to a valid DTPA investigation, particularly raising privacy concerns for its members and asserting First Amendment rights.
defendant_argument: The Attorney General argued that the CID was valid, reasonably based on PFLAG's executive director's affidavit, and necessary for investigating potential deceptive billing practices by medical providers circumventing SB 14, with privacy concerns addressed by allowing redactions.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Texas reversed the district court's "Final Declaratory Judgment and Injunction" and remanded the matter, ordering PFLAG to produce responsive documents subject to recognized privileges.

title: Paxton v. American Oversight
description: Whether district courts have jurisdiction to issue writs of mandamus against constitutional executive officers, such as the Governor and Attorney General, under the Public Information Act, with American Oversight arguing they do and the State arguing they do not.
plaintiff_argument: American Oversight contended that section 552.321(b) of the Public Information Act (PIA) was the Legislature's effort to empower district courts to issue writs of mandamus against constitutional executive officers, overriding the general limitation in section 22.002(c).
defendant_argument: The State argued that section 552.321(b) merely specifies the venue for PIA mandamus actions and does not expand district courts' jurisdiction over constitutional executive officers, which is exclusively reserved to the Supreme Court under section 22.002(c).
decision_outcome: The court reversed the judgment of the court of appeals and directed the district court to dismiss the mandamus petition for lack of jurisdiction, concluding that section 552.321(b) did not expand district courts' jurisdiction over constitutional executive officers.

title: Texas Department of Family & Protective Services v. Grassroots LeaderShip, Inc.
description: Whether Texas courts are constitutionally authorized to adjudicate moot cases that raise questions of considerable public importance, with the plaintiff arguing for such authorization via exceptions and the defendant arguing against it based on constitutional limits.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the case was not moot due to the possibility of re-detention, or alternatively, that the 'capable-of-repetition-yet-evading-review' or 'public-interest exception' should apply to allow the court to invalidate the rule.
defendant_argument: The defendant contended that the case was moot because the plaintiffs had been released, and that the 'public-interest exception' was not a valid constitutional basis for jurisdiction.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the court of appeals' judgment, vacated its judgment on the merits and the trial court's orders, and dismissed the case for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction because it was moot.

title: Ex Parte David Leonard Wood
description: Whether the Texas Constitution's due course of law and cruel and unusual punishment clauses prohibit the execution of individuals who are likely not guilty, and what standard of proof should apply to actual innocence claims in capital habeas corpus cases.
plaintiff_argument: The applicant argues that the Texas Constitution prohibits executing those who are likely not guilty, requiring a lower standard of proof (more likely than not) for actual innocence claims in capital cases, and that he should be granted access to DNA testing and a hearing on the merits of his new evidence.
defendant_argument: The state, through the court's previous rulings and statutory writ bar, maintains that the existing 'clear and convincing' standard for actual innocence claims is appropriate, and the majority's remand order, while allowing further evidence development, does not include specific guidance or a directive for DNA testing.
decision_outcome: The Court issued a remand to the lower court for further development of the evidence the Applicant presents, but without specific guidance or a directive for DNA testing.

title: Southern Methodist University v. South Central Jurisdictional Conference of the United Methodist Church
description: Whether Southern Methodist University (SMU) could unilaterally amend its articles of incorporation to remove the South Central Jurisdictional Conference's authority without the Conference's consent, or if Texas law and the church-autonomy doctrine protect the Conference's control.
plaintiff_argument: The Conference argued that SMU's articles of incorporation explicitly require Conference approval for amendments and that Texas law (§ 22.207) and the church-autonomy doctrine protect its right to control SMU.
defendant_argument: SMU argued it could amend its articles without the Conference's consent, that a general limitation on lawsuits (§ 20.002) prevented the Conference's challenge, and that the issue was a private matter not implicating church autonomy.
decision_outcome: The Court held that Texas law (§ 22.207) allows the South Central Jurisdictional Conference to seek judicial interpretation of SMU's articles of incorporation and proceed with its contract claim, thereby vindicating the Conference's rights.

title: Paxton v. Annunciation House
description: Whether the Attorney General has the constitutional and statutory authority to file a quo warranto action against Annunciation House for alleged violations of alien-harboring laws, and whether the state's records-request statutes are facially unconstitutional.
plaintiff_argument: The Attorney General argued that he has the constitutional and statutory authority to investigate Annunciation House for allegedly harboring illegal aliens and to file a quo warranto action to revoke its charter, and that the state's records-request statutes are constitutional.
defendant_argument: Annunciation House argued that the Attorney General's records request and proposed quo warranto action violated its constitutional rights, that the records-request statutes are unconstitutional, that the alien-harboring statutes are preempted by federal law or unconstitutionally vague, and that the action would violate the Texas Religious Freedom Restoration Act.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the trial court's denial of the Attorney General's motion for leave to file a quo warranto action, vacated the permanent injunction against records requests, and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: Stary v. Ethridge
description: Whether constitutional due process requires a clear and convincing evidence standard and consideration of the child's best interest for protective orders that prohibit parental contact for more than two years, or if a preponderance of the evidence standard is sufficient.
plaintiff_argument: Christine Stary argued that a lifetime protective order prohibiting contact with her children is tantamount to termination of parental rights, violating her fundamental due process rights by not requiring clear and convincing evidence.
defendant_argument: Brady Ethridge declined to appear. Amicus counsel argued that lengthy protective orders are not equivalent to parental rights termination because they do not divest all parental rights and allow for review.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Texas reversed the court of appeals' judgment and remanded the case to the trial court for a new hearing, holding that protective orders prohibiting parental contact for over two years require clear and convincing evidence and consideration of the child's best interest.

title: Commons of Lake Houston v. City of Houston
description: Whether the City of Houston's amended floodplain ordinance, which increased elevation requirements for construction, constitutes a compensable regulatory taking of The Commons's property, or if it is a valid exercise of police power and compliance with federal programs that cannot cause a taking.
plaintiff_argument: The Commons argued that the City's amended ordinance caused a regulatory taking of its property by rendering many lots undevelopable and destroying expected profits, requiring compensation under the Texas Constitution.
defendant_argument: The City argued that the amended ordinance was a valid exercise of its police power and designed to comply with the National Flood Insurance Program, thus it cannot constitute a compensable taking, and that The Commons's claim was unripe and it lacked standing.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the court of appeals' judgment, holding that a regulatory taking can occur even if the regulation is a valid exercise of police power or complies with a federal program, and remanded the case to the trial court for further proceedings, also finding the claim ripe and The Commons had standing.

title: Perez v. City of San Antonio
description: Whether Article I, Section 6-a of the Texas Constitution imposes a categorical bar on any limitation of any religious service, regardless of the sort of limitation and the government's interest in that limitation.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that Section 6-a imposes a categorical bar on any limitation of religious services, not even allowing the City to satisfy strict scrutiny.
defendant_argument: The City of San Antonio (implicitly, and as supported by the majority) argued that Section 6-a does not impose a categorical bar, and limitations are permissible, especially for government interests like preserving public lands.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that Article I, Section 6-a of the Texas Constitution does not impose a categorical bar on limitations of religious services that result from the government's preservation and maintenance of public lands.

title: Elliott v. City of College Station
description: Whether local regulation without a corresponding right to vote in local elections is incompatible with the Texas Constitution's "republican form of government" requirement, with plaintiffs arguing it is unconstitutional and defendants arguing it is a nonjusticiable political question.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs contend that local regulation over nonvoting extraterritorial jurisdiction (ETJ) residents is facially unconstitutional under the Texas Constitution's "republican form of government" limitation, and they seek a declaration that the ordinances are void.
defendant_argument: The City argues that the constitutional claim is not justiciable, asserting that the form of local government is a political question for the legislature, not the courts, and that the plaintiffs lack standing and their claims are not ripe.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the lower court judgments and remanded the case to the trial court with instructions to abate the proceedings, allowing the property owners a reasonable opportunity to complete the statutory opt-out process from the City's ETJ.

title: Ex parte Charette
description: Whether the Texas Ethics Commission (TEC) has exclusive jurisdiction over alleged campaign-law violations, requiring exhaustion of administrative remedies before criminal prosecution can proceed, or if prosecutors can initiate criminal charges independently.
plaintiff_argument: The prosecution was unauthorized because the Texas Ethics Commission (TEC) has exclusive jurisdiction over campaign-law violations, and its administrative process, including a referral for criminal prosecution, was a prerequisite that was not followed, thus violating her due process rights.
defendant_argument: District and county attorneys have constitutional authority to prosecute crimes, and the TEC's civil enforcement scheme does not grant it exclusive jurisdiction over criminal matters, nor does it prevent prosecutors from initiating criminal charges independently.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the court of appeals' judgment and ordered the dismissal of the indictments, holding that the trial court lacked subject matter jurisdiction because the TEC has exclusive jurisdiction over the initial determination of campaign law violations.

title: In re Dallas County
description: Whether Senate Bill 1045, which creates the Fifteenth Court of Appeals with statewide jurisdiction and mandates case transfers, is constitutional, with the plaintiff arguing it is unconstitutional due to its geographic range, jurisdictional scope, and judicial appointment process, and the defendant arguing it is constitutional.
plaintiff_argument: Dallas County argued that S.B. 1045 is unconstitutional because the Fifteenth Court's statewide geographic range, its jurisdictional scope, and the appointment process for its justices (who will not be elected until November 2026) violate the Texas Constitution.
defendant_argument: The State officials (HHSC) argued that S.B. 1045 is constitutional, asserting that the legislature has the authority to create the court and that the transfer of cases and the judicial appointment process are valid.
decision_outcome: The court denied Dallas County's petition for relief, holding that S.B. 1045 is constitutional and that the appeal must be transferred to the Fifteenth Court of Appeals as scheduled.

title: Borgelt v. Austin Firefighters Association
description: Whether Article 10 of the collective-bargaining agreement, which grants "Association Business Leave" to firefighters, violates the Texas Constitution's "Gift Clauses" by making an unconstitutional gift of public resources to a private party.
plaintiff_argument: Petitioners argue that Article 10, as written and/or implemented, violates the Gift Clauses because it impermissibly benefits the Austin Firefighters Association by providing paid leave for improper, private, or political purposes, without sufficient public control or return consideration.
defendant_argument: Respondents argue that Article 10 does not violate the Gift Clauses because it serves a legitimate public purpose, provides sufficient return consideration, and the City retains control over the funds, and that alleged improper uses are not authorized by the agreement itself.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that Article 10 of the collective-bargaining agreement does not facially violate the Gift Clauses, but reversed the award of fees and sanctions against the petitioners.

title: In re State
description: Whether Harris County's Uplift Harris program, which provides no-strings-attached cash payments to individuals, violates the Texas Constitution's prohibition on gratuitous payments or if it qualifies as a permissible economic development program.
plaintiff_argument: The State argues that the Uplift Harris program is unconstitutional as it constitutes "gratuitous payments to individuals" and lacks public control over the disbursed funds, violating the Texas Constitution.
defendant_argument: Harris County argues that the Uplift Harris program is a permissible exercise of its freedom to implement the program and qualifies as "economic development" under the Texas Constitution, section 52-a, as it aims to boost the economy.
decision_outcome: The court granted the State's motion for temporary relief, ordering Harris County to refrain from distributing funds under the Uplift Harris program until further order of the Court, pending the underlying appeal.

title: Texas Department of Transportation v. Self
description: Whether the Texas Department of Transportation (TxDOT) is immune from a negligence claim for trees cut by a subcontractor and whether TxDOT intentionally destroyed private property for public use, thus constituting inverse condemnation.
plaintiff_argument: The Selfs argued that TxDOT was negligent because subcontractor employees were TxDOT employees or TxDOT employees operated the equipment, and that TxDOT intentionally directed the destruction of their trees, constituting inverse condemnation.
defendant_argument: TxDOT argued sovereign immunity for negligence because subcontractor employees were not TxDOT employees and TxDOT employees did not operate the equipment, and for inverse condemnation because TxDOT did not intend to damage property outside its right-of-way.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the court of appeals' judgment, dismissing the negligence cause of action against TxDOT but remanding the inverse condemnation claim to the trial court for further proceedings.

title: Hogan v. Southern Methodist University
description: Whether the application of the Pandemic Liability Protection Act to Luke Hogan's breach-of-contract claim violates the retroactivity clause in article I, section 16 of the Texas Constitution, with Hogan arguing it does and Southern Methodist University arguing it does not.
plaintiff_argument: Hogan contended that the Pandemic Liability Protection Act (PLPA) retroactively withdrew his right to hold SMU liable for breaking its promise of in-person education, violating the Texas Constitution's prohibition on retroactive laws, as he had a settled expectation of monetary recovery.
defendant_argument: Southern Methodist University (SMU) argued that the PLPA protects schools from monetary liability for altering activities due to pandemic-related government orders, that the common-law impossibility doctrine would have limited its liability anyway, and that Hogan had no settled expectation of a refund.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the application of the Pandemic Liability Protection Act to Hogan's breach-of-contract claim does not violate the retroactivity clause in article I, section 16 of the Texas Constitution.

title: Texas v. Loe
description: Whether the Legislature's prohibition of certain medical treatments for children suffering from gender dysphoria violates the Texas Constitution, with plaintiffs arguing it infringes on parental rights, physicians' occupational freedom, and discriminates against transgender adolescents, while defendants argue it is a constitutional and rational policy choice to regulate medicine and protect children.
plaintiff_argument: The statute is unconstitutional because it infringes on parents' fundamental right to make medical decisions for their children, deprives Texas physicians of their occupational freedom, and discriminates against transgender adolescents based on sex, sex stereotypes, and transgender status.
defendant_argument: The statute is a permissible and rational policy choice by the Legislature to regulate the practice of medicine and protect the health and wellbeing of children, and it does not unconstitutionally infringe on parental rights, physicians' occupational freedom, or discriminate.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Texas reversed and vacated the trial court's temporary injunction order, concluding that the plaintiffs failed to establish a probable right to relief on any of their asserted constitutional violations.

title: City of Dallas v. Employees Retirement Fund of City of Dallas
description: Whether a city ordinance may bestow on a third party the perpetual right to veto categories of future lawmaking.
plaintiff_argument: The City of Dallas argued that its ordinance imposing term limits on the Fund's board was valid because the board's veto power was an unconstitutional delegation of legislative authority and therefore unenforceable.
defendant_argument: The Employees' Retirement Fund argued that its governing chapter was a "trust document" requiring board consent for amendments, and the City's term-limit ordinance was an invalid amendment without such consent.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the court of appeals' judgment, holding that the board's veto power over city law is unenforceable because a legislative body cannot bind its successors or alienate its lawmaking authority.

title: Becerra v. State
description: Whether an alternate juror's presence and participation, including voting, in jury deliberations violates constitutional or statutory provisions, and if so, what standard of harm applies.
plaintiff_argument: The alternate juror's participation and vote violated his constitutional right to a twelve-person jury and statutory prohibitions against unauthorized persons in deliberations, requiring a new trial with a presumption of harm.
defendant_argument: Any error from the alternate juror's presence was either waived or harmless, and the presumption of harm was rebutted.
decision_outcome: The court found that the alternate juror's presence and participation in deliberations violated statutory prohibitions (Article 36.22) but not constitutional or other statutory provisions regarding jury composition, and remanded the case for the court of appeals to conduct a statutory harm analysis.

title: Hensley v. State Commission on Judicial Conduct
description: Whether a judge is required to exhaust administrative remedies before suing the State Commission on Judicial Conduct for alleged violations of the Texas Religious Freedom Restoration Act (TRFRA) after receiving a public warning.
plaintiff_argument: The judge argued that she was not required to exhaust administrative remedies because her suit was not a collateral attack on the warning and the administrative process could not provide the relief she sought.
defendant_argument: The State Commission on Judicial Conduct argued that the judge failed to exhaust her administrative remedies, which was a jurisdictional prerequisite to her suit, and therefore the district court lacked jurisdiction.
decision_outcome: The court held that the judge was not required to exhaust her administrative remedies before filing her suit against the Commission.

title: Zurawski v. Texas
description: Whether Texas's Human Life Protection Act, as currently interpreted, unconstitutionally restricts access to life-saving abortions, or if it adequately permits abortions when a woman's life or major bodily function is at risk.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that Texas's abortion laws are unclear and too restrictive, causing physicians to delay or deny medically necessary abortions, and that the law should permit abortions in broader circumstances, including for "unsafe" pregnancies or when the fetus is unlikely to survive.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that Texas law already permits life-saving abortions when a physician, exercising reasonable medical judgment, determines a life-threatening physical condition places the mother at risk of death or serious physical impairment, and that the trial court's injunction incorrectly broadened the law's exceptions without constitutional justification.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the trial court's temporary injunction, ruling that the Human Life Protection Act permits abortions when a physician, using reasonable medical judgment, determines a life-threatening physical condition places the woman at risk of death or serious physical impairment, and that the Act does not violate the Texas Constitution.

title: Harris County v. Texas
description: Whether Senate Bill 1750, which reorganizes election administration in Harris County, is an unconstitutional local law, with Harris County arguing it is unconstitutional and would cause irreparable harm to election administration, while the State Officer Defendants implicitly argue for its enforcement.
plaintiff_argument: Harris County argues that Senate Bill 1750 is an unconstitutional local law that would cause imminent and irreparable injury by disrupting election administration, leading to inefficiencies, disorganization, confusion, and increased costs, and jeopardizing the validity of the November Election.
defendant_argument: The State Officer Defendants (Interim Attorney General and Secretary of State) implicitly argue for the enforcement of Senate Bill 1750, which would abolish the Harris County Elections Administrator position and transfer its responsibilities, suggesting it is a valid law.
decision_outcome: The court granted Harris County's request for a temporary injunction, preventing the State Officer Defendants from enforcing Senate Bill 1750 until all issues in the lawsuit are finally determined.

title: Ex parte Sheffield
description: Whether speedy trial claims are cognizable in pretrial habeas corpus, particularly when a trial is indefinitely postponed due to administrative orders.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that his speedy trial claim was cognizable in pretrial habeas corpus under the Ex parte Perry rule because the indefinite delay in jury trials due to COVID-19 emergency orders violated his right to a speedy trial, which would be effectively undermined if not vindicated before trial.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that speedy trial claims are not cognizable in pretrial habeas corpus because allowing such claims would improperly lead to interlocutory appeals, inject appellate delay, and thus undermine the speedy trial right, suggesting mandamus as the proper remedy.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the judgment of the court of appeals, holding that speedy trial claims are not cognizable in pretrial habeas corpus, and the Perry rule does not apply to such claims, clarifying that mandamus is the proper remedy for indefinitely postponed trials.

title: Hotze v. Turner
description: Whether a city's "primacy clause" requiring a citizen-initiated charter amendment to receive more votes than a council-initiated amendment to become effective, and the city's discretion to delay the effective date of an adopted amendment, conflict with state law requiring adoption by a simple majority vote and immediate effectiveness upon declaration of adoption.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the primacy clause violates state law by imposing a higher vote threshold for citizen-initiated amendments and that the city cannot indefinitely delay the effectiveness of an adopted amendment. The plaintiff also contended that the two approved propositions could be harmonized.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the primacy clause does not conflict with state law because the statute only requires adoption, not immediate effectiveness, and that the city has discretion over an amendment's effective date. The defendant also claimed the two propositions irreconcilably conflict, and the city's charter dictates that Proposition 1 prevails.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the judgment of the court of appeals in part, ruling that the city's primacy clause is void for conflicting with state law and that an adopted amendment becomes effective when the municipality declares its adoption. The court affirmed the trial court's ruling that the city complied with Proposition 1 and remanded the case to determine how to harmonize the two propositions.

title: City of Houston v. Houston Proffesional Fire Fighters Association
description: Whether Chapter 174 of the Local Government Code, which governs firefighter collective bargaining and compensation standards, is constitutional and waives governmental immunity, and whether it preempts a local pay-parity amendment.
plaintiff_argument: The Houston Professional Fire Fighters' Association argued that Chapter 174 is constitutional, waives the City's governmental immunity, and its state-level compensation standards preempt the local pay-parity amendment.
defendant_argument: The City of Houston and the Houston Police Officers' Union argued that Chapter 174's judicial-enforcement provisions violate the separation of powers, that the City is immune from suit, and that Chapter 174 does not preempt the local pay-parity amendment.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the lower court's ruling that Chapter 174 is constitutional and waives the City's immunity, and reversed the lower court's ruling on preemption, holding that Chapter 174 preempts the local pay-parity amendment.

title: The Lilith Fund for Reproductive Equity v. Dickson
description: Whether statements equating abortion to murder and characterizing abortion providers as "criminal" are defamatory false statements of fact or constitutionally protected opinions in the context of public debate.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the defendant's statements falsely characterized abortion as murder and labeled them "criminal organizations," which is legally defamatory because abortion was not murder under Texas law at the time.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued his statements were protected opinions about abortion law and its interpretation, made in pursuit of changing the law, and thus not defamatory.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Texas affirmed the dismissal of the defamation suit, holding that the challenged statements were protected opinion about abortion law and free speech, not verifiable false statements of fact.

title: Virlar v. Puente
description: Whether Chapter 33 of the Civil Practice and Remedies Code requires a credit for a family member's settlement against the judgment, and whether Chapter 74 of the Texas Medical Liability Act requires periodic payments of damages for future medical expenses.
plaintiff_argument: Puente argued that her daughter's settlement should not be credited against her damages and that periodic payments for future medical expenses were not required.
defendant_argument: Virlar and Gonzaba argued that Chapter 33 required a credit for the daughter's settlement and that the TMLA required periodic payments for future medical expenses.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the court of appeals' judgment in part, holding that the trial court improperly denied a credit for C.P.'s settlement and an award of periodic payments for future medical expenses, and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: State v. Aktiengesellschaft
description: Whether the Governor's appointment of substitute justices to the Supreme Court of Texas, in a case where the State is a party, violates due process or creates an appearance of impropriety, thereby requiring the Chief Justice to withdraw the certification letter and dismiss the petitions.
plaintiff_argument: The State of Texas implicitly argued that the Governor's appointment of substitute justices is a valid statutory process that does not violate due process or create an appearance of partiality, and therefore, the Respondents' requests should be denied.
defendant_argument: The Respondents argued that allowing the Governor to appoint justices in this case would create due-process and ethical problems, effectively allowing the State to "be the judge of its own cause," and that the Chief Justice should rescind the request and dismiss the petitions.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Texas denied the Respondents' requests to withdraw the Chief Justice's certification letter and to dismiss the petitions as improvidently granted, ruling that the Governor's appointment of substitute justices does not create a serious risk of actual bias or violate due-process provisions.

title: Nath v. Texas Children's Hospital
description: Whether a party sanctioned with attorney's fees has a constitutional right to a jury trial to determine the reasonableness and necessity of those fees.
plaintiff_argument: Dr. Nath argues he is entitled to a jury finding on the amount of attorney's fees the Hospital and Baylor reasonably and necessarily incurred, as this is a question of fact.
defendant_argument: The Hospital and Baylor argue that the law-of-the-case doctrine bars Nath's request for a jury trial, or that he waived the complaint.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Texas denied the petition for review, thereby affirming the lower court's decision to deny Dr. Nath a jury trial on the attorney's fees sanction.

title: Texas Department of State Health Services v. Crown Distributing LLC
description: Whether the Texas law prohibiting the processing and manufacturing of smokable hemp products violates the Texas Constitution's due-course clause, with plaintiffs arguing it infringes on economic liberty and defendants arguing the clause does not protect this specific interest.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs, Hemp Companies, argued that the state's ban on manufacturing and processing smokable hemp products violates the Texas Constitution's due-course clause because it lacks a rational connection to governmental interest and is oppressive, infringing on their right to economic liberty and to work in a lawful calling.
defendant_argument: The defendants, Texas Department of State Health Services, argued that the due-course clause does not protect the Hemp Companies' interest in manufacturing or processing smokable hemp products, as they are complaining about the inability to produce products in contravention of a long-standing law, not a lawful calling.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Texas reversed the trial court's judgment, concluding that the due-course clause does not protect the interest asserted by the Hemp Companies in manufacturing and processing smokable hemp products.

title: Abbott v. Mexican American Legislative Caucus
description: Whether Texas's reapportionment laws (H.B. 1 and S.B. 4) violate Article III, Sections 26 and 28 of the Texas Constitution, with plaintiffs arguing they do and defendants arguing they do not.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that H.B. 1 violates the county-line rule (Article III, Section 26) by not providing enough wholly contained districts for Cameron County, and that H.B. 1 and S.B. 4 violate Article III, Section 28 by being enacted during a special session rather than the first regular session after the census.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the plaintiffs lacked standing, their claims were moot, and were barred by sovereign immunity, asserting that the reapportionment laws complied with constitutional requirements or that Section 28 did not prohibit apportionment at other times.
decision_outcome: The court dismissed the Mexican American Legislative Caucus's claims and the Gutierrez Plaintiffs' Section 28 claim for lack of jurisdiction, but remanded the Gutierrez Plaintiffs' Section 26 claim to the trial court for repleading against a proper defendant.

title: Fire Protection Service v. Survitec Survival Products
description: Whether the application of the Fair Practices of Equipment Manufacturers, Distributors, Wholesalers, and Dealers Act to a preexisting at-will agreement violates the Texas Constitution's prohibition against retroactive laws.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, FPS, argued that the Act should apply to the agreement and that Survitec's constitutional challenge was improperly brought under the retroactivity clause instead of the contracts clause, and that Survitec violated the Act by terminating their agreement without good cause.
defendant_argument: The defendant, Survitec, argued that applying the Act to their preexisting at-will agreement unconstitutionally retroactively eliminated their right to terminate the relationship at will, and that the grace period provided was insufficient notice to adapt to the new law.
decision_outcome: The court concluded that the application of the Act to Survitec's termination of the agreement does not violate the constitutional prohibition against retroactive laws.

title: City of Baytown v. Schrock
description: Whether the City of Baytown's utility enforcement actions, which caused economic harm to Alan Schrock's property, constitute a regulatory taking requiring compensation under the Texas or United States Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The city's actions, including withholding utility service and placing a lien, resulted in loss of rental income and property disrepair, which constitutes a taking in violation of the Texas or United States Constitution, or alternatively, a physical taking or exaction.
defendant_argument: The city's enforcement actions were not an intentional taking for public use but a means to collect unpaid utility bills, and Schrock failed to demonstrate that the enforcement of municipal ordinances, which do not regulate property use, constitutes a regulatory taking.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the court of appeals' judgment and reinstated the trial court's directed verdict, ruling that the city's utility enforcement actions do not establish a regulatory taking of private property as a matter of law.

title: State v. Stephens
description: Whether Section 273.021 of the Texas Election Code, which authorizes the Attorney General (AG) to prosecute election law offenses, violates the Texas Constitution's Separation of Powers Clause, with the plaintiff arguing it does and the defendant arguing it does not.
plaintiff_argument: The Attorney General lacked constitutional authority to independently prosecute election law offenses, violating the separation of powers, and therefore the indictment against her should be dismissed.
defendant_argument: The Attorney General has the authority to prosecute election law offenses, and the Court's original opinion finding a constitutional violation and ordering dismissal of the indictment was flawed and should be reconsidered.
decision_outcome: The Court denied the Attorney General's motion for rehearing, thereby upholding its original decision that Section 273.021 of the Texas Election Code, which authorizes the AG to prosecute election law offenses, violates the Texas Constitution's Separation of Powers Clause, and maintaining the dismissal of Stephens's indictment.

title: In re Abbott
description: Whether the Texas Constitution grants the House of Representatives the authority to physically compel the attendance of absent members, with the plaintiffs arguing it only allows persuasion and dialogue, and the defendants arguing it authorizes physical compulsion including arrest.
plaintiff_argument: The House's power to "compel the attendance of absent members" authorizes only persuasion and dialogue, not physical compulsion or arrest, and that such compulsion would violate statutory and constitutional protections.
defendant_argument: The Texas Constitution clearly empowers the House to "compel the attendance of absent members" through physical compulsion, including arrest, to secure a quorum, and this power is committed to the legislature's discretion.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the Texas Constitution grants the House of Representatives the authority to physically compel the attendance of absent members and directed the district court to withdraw the temporary restraining order that prohibited such actions.

title: Odyssey 2020 Academy, Inc. v. Galveston Central Appraisal District
description: Whether property leased by a public open-enrollment charter school, though deemed "public property for all purposes" by statute, qualifies for a tax exemption under the Texas Constitution when the underlying fee interest is privately owned.
plaintiff_argument: Odyssey contends that property it leases with state funds is "public property for all purposes" under Education Code section 12.128(a), and therefore qualifies for tax exemptions under Tax Code section 11.11 and various constitutional provisions that exempt publicly owned property or property devoted exclusively to public use.
defendant_argument: The District argues that Odyssey only has a leasehold interest, not actual ownership, and the Constitution does not permit the Legislature to recharacterize privately owned property as publicly owned for tax exemption purposes, nor does public use alone suffice for exemption without public ownership.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Texas affirmed the lower courts' judgments, ruling that Odyssey 2020 Academy, Inc. is not entitled to an exemption from ad valorem taxes on the privately owned property it leases.

title: Texas State University v. Villarreal
description: Whether a state university's dismissal of a student for poor academic performance implicates a liberty or property interest protected by the Texas Constitution's guarantee of due course of law.
plaintiff_argument: Villarreal argued that his academic dismissal, stemming from the university's mishandling of a cheating investigation, deprived him of his liberty and property interests in his graduate education without due course of law, violating the Texas Constitution.
defendant_argument: Texas Southern University argued that academic dismissal for poor performance does not implicate a protected liberty or property interest under the Texas Constitution, and even if it did, the procedures followed were constitutionally adequate.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the court of appeals' judgment, holding that academic dismissal for poor performance does not implicate a protected liberty interest and that the university provided adequate procedural due course of law, thereby dismissing Villarreal's constitutional claims.

title: Texas Propane Gas Association v. City of Houston
description: Whether civil courts have subject-matter jurisdiction to adjudicate a preemption claim against local regulations that carry criminal penalties, and whether the Texas Propane Gas Association (TPGA) has standing to challenge all of the City of Houston's liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) regulations en masse.
plaintiff_argument: The Texas Propane Gas Association (TPGA) argued that the City of Houston's local LPG regulations are preempted by state law and that civil courts have jurisdiction to hear its preemption claim, even if the local regulations include criminal penalties, as the essence of the case is civil and threatens irreparable injury to property rights. TPGA also argued it has standing to challenge all the City's LPG regulations due to the burden of inconsistent local rules.
defendant_argument: The City of Houston argued that civil courts lack subject-matter jurisdiction because its local LPG regulations carry criminal penalties, making it a 'criminal law matter' that should be raised in defense to prosecution. The City also contended that TPGA lacks standing to challenge all its LPG regulations without demonstrating specific injury for each discrete regulation challenged.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the judgment of the court of appeals, ruling that civil courts have subject-matter jurisdiction over TPGA's preemption claim and that TPGA has standing to challenge the City's LPG regulations, and remanded the case to the trial court for further proceedings.

title: Dulin v. State
description: Whether the "time payment fee" was prematurely assessed, and if an appeal suspends the obligation to pay court costs, thereby suspending the clock for the fee.
plaintiff_argument: The time payment fee was unconstitutional due to separation of powers, and/or prematurely assessed.
defendant_argument: The time payment fee was prematurely assessed (but for a different reason than the court of appeals), or it was a legitimate and constitutional court cost.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the time payment fee was prematurely assessed because an appeal suspends the obligation to pay court costs, thus suspending the clock for the fee. The judgment of the court of appeals was vacated and the case remanded.
